rationale: A wins because it keeps the story honest while still giving the founder three usable doors: founder lineage, category thesis, and investor thesis. Its best line, "An unnamed 'climate-focused seed fund' cannot anchor a VC-thesis story," is the kind of useful brutality that prevents a bad pitch from leaving the building. B has good instincts, but "Community-solar grids are hitting a load-balancing wall" and "keep community-solar grids from buckling" spend proof the update does not have. That is how you turn a thin but real seed story into an editor's eye-roll.
gaps_in_A: "Community solar is growing. The software to coordinate it isn't." This may be true, but the update does not prove growth or a software shortage. A correctly asks for proof, but the headline still overcommits.
"one co-founder came from Tesla Energy's commercial grid-scale deployment side" adds role color the update did not provide. The set later asks for confirmed roles, so it knows the floor is missing.
"community solar will scale, coordination software is the bottleneck, and a startup can own that market" is a useful thesis, but it is still an inferred VC argument until the fund says it on record.
gaps_in_B: "keep community-solar grids from buckling" is melodrama without evidence. The update says grid strain; it does not say buckling.
"someone who ran systems inside Tesla Energy" invents a job function. Ex-Tesla Energy is a credential, not a title.

"Community-solar grids are hitting a load-balancing wall — and software is the cheap fix being tried" is the big offense. No independent results, no grid-strain event, no proof software is cheaper than grid upgrades.
"now starting a company at the seam between the two" is vague consultant fog. It sounds clever and says almost nothing.
